findings.bug: The case for "off" returns Boolean.TRUE instead of Boolean.FALSE.
findings.why_real: The method's own Javadoc says it supports 'on'/'off' pairs, and the sibling cases are consistent ("on"->TRUE, "no"->FALSE, '0'->FALSE, "false"->FALSE). "off" is a falsey token, so returning TRUE is a clear copy-paste defect (should be Boolean.FALSE).
findings.how_to_prove: assertEquals(Boolean.FALSE, StringUtils.toBoolean("off")); currently returns Boolean.TRUE. Also StringUtils.toBoolean("off", true) returns true instead of false.

findings.bug: The version segment is appended based on whether the GROUP is non-empty (isNotEmpty(group)) rather than whether the VERSION is non-empty, so a group-only service produces 'group/interface:null' and a version-only service silently drops its version.
findings.why_real: The canonical Dubbo service key format is group/interface:version. The append at line 916 uses the value of `version` but is guarded by isNotEmpty(group) (line 915) — an obvious copy-paste of the group guard on line 910. Correct guard is isNotEmpty(version).
findings.how_to_prove: Map m={GROUP_KEY:"g", INTERFACE_KEY:"com.I"} (no version) -> expected "g/com.I", actual "g/com.I:null". Map m2={INTERFACE_KEY:"com.I", VERSION_KEY:"1.0"} (no group) -> expected "com.I:1.0", actual "com.I" (version dropped).

findings.bug: randomSelectOne computes `int rate = originSize / cardinality` with no guard for cardinality == 0, throwing ArithmeticException (/ by zero) on a non-empty BitList whose elements all live in tailList.
findings.why_real: A BitList can be non-empty (size() > 0) while rootSet.cardinality() == 0: construct empty (rootSet unset) then addToTailList(e). size() = cardinality + tailSize > 0 makes randomSelectOne a legitimate call, but line 160 divides originSize by cardinality(0) before ever consulting tailList.
findings.how_to_prove: BitList<String> b = new BitList<>(new ArrayList<>(List.of("a")), true); b.addToTailList("x"); b.randomSelectOne(); -> throws ArithmeticException("/ by zero") instead of returning "x".

findings.bug: Deserialization assumes a single InputStream.read(bytes,0,length) call reads exactly `length` bytes and throws IllegalArgumentException when `read != length`, but InputStream.read is only contractually required to read *some* bytes (up to length), so a payload split across multiple reads (e.g. a network/chunked stream) fails spuriously.
findings.why_real: Per java.io.InputStream#read(byte[],int,int) Javadoc, the method reads 'up to len bytes' and 'may return fewer' even when more data will arrive; only readNBytes / DataInputStream.readFully guarantee a full read. Lines 96, 114, 153, and 197 all use the single-read pattern and reject any short read.
findings.how_to_prove: Wrap the JSONB bytes in an InputStream whose read(b,off,len) returns at most 1 byte per call (or a slow socket stream); readObject throws IllegalArgumentException("expected read length ... but actual read: 1") even though all bytes are ultimately available. A correct impl (readNBytes) returns the object.
